items.title: Physical geography — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the physical geography guide.

cards.front: Which ocean is the largest and deepest?
cards.back:
Pacific

It is also the oldest ocean floor.

cards.front: What share of Earth's water is held by the oceans?
cards.back:
About 97%

Rivers and lakes hold less than 1%.

cards.front: What is the deepest point of the ocean called?
cards.back:
The Mariana Trench

It lies in the western Pacific.

cards.front: Roughly how fast do tectonic plates move?
cards.back:
A few centimetres per year

About as fast as a fingernail grows.

cards.front: What forms where two plates pull apart?
cards.back:
A rift, often filled by a new ocean

The East African Rift is an example.

cards.front: Why are the poles colder than the equator?
cards.back:
Sunlight strikes them at a slant

The same energy is spread over a wider area.

cards.front: Which current keeps north-western Europe mild?
cards.back:
The Gulf Stream

It carries warm water north-east across the Atlantic.

cards.front: What percentage of the Earth's surface is covered by water?
cards.back:
About 71%

Most of it is salt water.

cards.front: Which two continents fit together like puzzle pieces?
cards.back:
Africa and South America

They were joined in Pangaea.

cards.front: What instrument measures the strength of an earthquake?
cards.back:
A seismograph

It records ground motion over time.

items.title: Turning points of history — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the turning points of history guide.

cards.front: Where did writing first appear, around 3200 BCE?
cards.back:
Mesopotamia

It began as accounting records.

cards.front: What made movable type revolutionary in Europe?
cards.back:
It made copies far cheaper to produce

Printed arguments spread faster than censorship.

cards.front: Which invention moved production into factories?
cards.back:
The steam engine

Steam power no longer depended on a river.

cards.front: Why did the first cities grow beside rivers?
cards.back:
Flooding left fertile soil and a food surplus

Surplus food let people specialise.

cards.front: What did the printing press make possible for learning?
cards.back:
Widely shared, identical texts

Errors could be corrected once and reprinted.

cards.front: Which ancient library is famous for collecting the ancient world's texts?
cards.back:
The Library of Alexandria

Its decline remains debated.

cards.front: What was the Silk Road?
cards.back:
A network of trade routes between Asia and Europe

Goods travelled with ideas and technologies.

cards.front: Which document limited the power of the English king in 1215?
cards.back:
Magna Carta

It established that the king was subject to law.

cards.front: What was the Renaissance a revival of?
cards.back:
Classical learning and art

It began in the Italian city-states.

cards.front: Which empire built the road network later used across Europe?
cards.back:
The Roman Empire

Some routes are still in use.

items.title: Everyday science — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the everyday science guide.

cards.front: What is the smallest unit of life?
cards.back:
The cell

Some organisms are a single cell.

cards.front: What does DNA carry?
cards.back:
The instructions for building and running a cell

Almost every cell in a body holds the same DNA.

cards.front: What happens to energy in any process?
cards.back:
It is converted, never destroyed

The total amount stays constant.

cards.front: Which way does heat flow?
cards.back:
From warmer to colder

A fridge moves heat the other way by doing work.

cards.front: What does a catalyst do?
cards.back:
Speeds a reaction without being consumed

Enzymes are biological catalysts.

cards.front: What is a molecule?
cards.back:
Two or more atoms bonded together

Water is one oxygen and two hydrogen atoms.

cards.front: What is photosynthesis for?
cards.back:
Turning light into chemical energy

Plants, algae and some bacteria do it.

cards.front: What gas do plants take from the air to grow?
cards.back:
Carbon dioxide

They release oxygen as a by-product.

cards.front: What is the pH of a neutral solution?
cards.back:
7

Below 7 is acidic, above is basic.

cards.front: Which force keeps planets in orbit?
cards.back:
Gravity

It weakens with the square of the distance.

items.title: How the web works — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the how the web works guide.

cards.front: What does DNS do?
cards.back:
Translates a domain name into an IP address

It is a distributed hierarchy.

cards.front: What does HTTPS add to HTTP?
cards.back:
Encryption and proof of the server's identity

It runs over TLS.

cards.front: What does HTTP status 404 mean?
cards.back:
The resource does not exist

410 means it existed and is gone.

cards.front: What is a cookie used for?
cards.back:
Keeping state between requests

HTTP itself is stateless.

cards.front: What is the role of a web browser?
cards.back:
Requesting, rendering and running pages

It also enforces security policies.

cards.front: Why is an open web standard important?
cards.back:
Anyone can implement it, so no vendor controls access

Interoperability comes from shared specifications.

cards.front: What is an API?
cards.back:
A defined way for programs to exchange data

It is a contract, not a UI.

cards.front: What does a CDN do?
cards.back:
Serves files from a location near the visitor

It reduces latency.

cards.front: What is the difference between a domain and a URL?
cards.back:
A domain names a host; a URL locates a resource on it

The URL adds scheme, path and query.

cards.front: What does JSON represent?
cards.back:
Structured data as nested keys and values

It is readable by humans and machines.

items.title: How language models work — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the how language models work guide.

cards.front: What is a token in a language model?
cards.back:
A piece of text, shorter than a word on average

Rare words are split into several tokens.

cards.front: What does a language model actually predict?
cards.back:
The next token

Everything else emerges from that.

cards.front: What is a hallucination?
cards.back:
A confident answer that is not supported by facts

It follows from predicting plausible text.

cards.front: What does the context window limit?
cards.back:
How much text the model can consider at once

Older turns fall out of it.

cards.front: What is a prompt?
cards.back:
The instruction and context given to a model

Clarity beats cleverness.

cards.front: Why does giving a source document help?
cards.back:
It grounds the answer in text the model can quote

Retrieval reduces invented facts.

cards.front: What is fine-tuning?
cards.back:
Further training on a narrower set of examples

It shapes style and task behaviour.

cards.front: What does temperature control?
cards.back:
How random the next-token choice is

Low temperature is more deterministic.

cards.front: What is an embedding?
cards.back:
A vector that places a text by its meaning

Similar meanings lie close together.

cards.front: Why must a model's output be verified?
cards.back:
It optimises for plausibility, not truth

Check against a source outside the model.

items.title: Sport and training — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the sport and training guide.

cards.front: Which system powers a short, maximal sprint?
cards.back:
Stored energy used without oxygen

It lasts a few seconds.

cards.front: When does the body adapt to training?
cards.back:
During recovery between sessions

Fatigue is the stimulus, rest is the adaptation.

cards.front: What does aerobic training improve?
cards.back:
The ability to use oxygen over long efforts

It builds the heart and the capillary network.

cards.front: Why is sleep part of a training plan?
cards.back:
It is when most recovery happens

Short sleep blunts adaptation.

cards.front: What is progressive overload?
cards.back:
Gradually increasing the demand of training

Small increments are sustainable.

cards.front: What does a warm-up prepare?
cards.back:
Muscles, joints and the cardiovascular system for effort

It also rehearses the movement.

cards.front: Why do varied repetitions improve a skill?
cards.back:
They build a general pattern, not one fixed motion

Too much variation prevents refinement.

cards.front: What is carbohydrate loading for?
cards.back:
Filling glycogen stores before a long effort

It matters for endurance events.

cards.front: What is a common sign of overtraining?
cards.back:
Resting heart rate rising and performance falling

It needs rest, not more work.

cards.front: What does hydration affect first?
cards.back:
Blood volume and the ability to regulate heat

Thirst arrives late.

items.title: Reading a work of art — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the reading a work of art guide.

cards.front: What does composition describe in a picture?
cards.back:
How the elements are arranged in the frame

It directs the viewer's eye.

cards.front: Which colours tend to advance towards the viewer?
cards.back:
Warm colours

Cool tones recede.

cards.front: What is chiaroscuro?
cards.back:
Strong contrast between light and dark

Caravaggio used it dramatically.

cards.front: Why does context matter for a work of art?
cards.back:
It explains what the work answered to

Patronage and censorship shape what is made.

cards.front: What is a vanishing point?
cards.back:
Where parallel lines appear to meet in perspective

It creates depth on a flat surface.

cards.front: What does a novel's narrator control?
cards.back:
What the reader can know, and when

An unreliable narrator makes this visible.

cards.front: What is the difference between story and plot?
cards.back:
Story is the events; plot is their arrangement

Order changes meaning.

cards.front: What does negative space do?
cards.back:
Gives the subject room and emphasis

Silence works the same way in music.

cards.front: Why do museums group works by period?
cards.back:
Shared constraints and conventions become visible

It shows what changed, and when.

cards.front: What is a motif in literature?
cards.back:
A recurring element that carries meaning

Repetition builds significance.

items.title: Health literacy — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the health literacy guide.

cards.front: What is absolute risk?
cards.back:
How many people in a group are affected

It is the number that matters to a patient.

cards.front: What is relative risk?
cards.back:
How much a rate changes between groups

A doubling of a small number stays small.

cards.front: What makes a randomised trial stronger?
cards.back:
Participants are assigned to groups by chance

Chance assignment limits bias.

cards.front: What is a placebo effect?
cards.back:
An improvement caused by expectation, not the treatment

Blinding is used to control for it.

cards.front: Why do reviews pool several studies?
cards.back:
A larger base gives a more stable estimate

They also show disagreement.

cards.front: What does 'statistically significant' mean?
cards.back:
The result is unlikely to be chance alone

Significance is not clinical importance.

cards.front: Why is a control group needed?
cards.back:
To show what would have happened without the treatment

Comparison is what creates evidence.

cards.front: What is a confounding factor?
cards.back:
Something else that differs between groups and explains the result

Randomisation spreads such factors out.

cards.front: Why can a headline about risk mislead?
cards.back:
It reports relative change without the baseline

Ask how many people, out of how many.

cards.front: What does prevalence describe?
cards.back:
How many people have a condition at a time

Incidence counts new cases.

items.title: Everyday mathematics — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the everyday mathematics guide.

cards.front: What does a percentage express?
cards.back:
A fraction of a hundred

It makes comparisons easier.

cards.front: A 20% rise after a 20% fall: where are you?
cards.back:
Below the starting value

The fall applies to a larger number.

cards.front: How do you combine two independent probabilities?
cards.back:
Multiply them

Two coin flips: half of a half.

cards.front: What is the median?
cards.back:
The middle value of a sorted list

It resists extreme values.

cards.front: What does a 1-in-1000 risk mean?
cards.back:
About one case per thousand people

The base matters more than the ratio.

cards.front: What is the mean of 2, 4 and 9?
cards.back:
5

Add and divide by the count.

cards.front: Why estimate before calculating exactly?
cards.back:
It catches order-of-magnitude errors

Rounding to one figure is enough.

cards.front: What is a proportion?
cards.back:
A statement that two ratios are equal

It allows scaling of recipes and maps.

cards.front: If a car covers 120 km in 1.5 h, what is its average speed?
cards.back:
80 km/h

Distance divided by time.

cards.front: What does multiplication by a number below 1 do?
cards.back:
Reduces the value

Percentages are decimals in disguise.

items.title: Climate and resources — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the climate and resources guide.

cards.front: What makes CO2 a greenhouse gas?
cards.back:
It absorbs infrared radiation and re-emits it

More of it raises the surface temperature.

cards.front: Which sector consumes the most fresh water?
cards.back:
Agriculture

Irrigation dominates.

cards.front: What is the difference between kW and kWh?
cards.back:
Power versus energy over time

A kilowatt-hour is one kilowatt for an hour.

cards.front: Why is fresh water a limited resource?
cards.back:
Only a small share of water is fresh and reachable

Distribution matters as much as volume.

cards.front: What does an energy transition need besides generation?
cards.back:
Grids, storage and flexible demand

A supply is only useful if it arrives when needed.

cards.front: What is biodiversity?
cards.back:
The variety of living things in a place

It supports resilience.

cards.front: Why do trees help a city?
cards.back:
They shade, cool air and slow storm water

Urban heat islands are measurable.

cards.front: What is a carbon budget?
cards.back:
The total emissions that fit a temperature limit

It is spent once.

cards.front: What does recycling save most effectively?
cards.back:
The energy of making a material from scratch

Aluminium is the classic case.

cards.front: Why does eating less meat reduce emissions?
cards.back:
Livestock uses land and feed with high emissions

The effect varies by production method.

items.title: Economics in plain words — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the economics in plain words guide.

cards.front: What does inflation measure?
cards.back:
The change in a basket of prices over time

The basket decides the result.

cards.front: What is interest?
cards.back:
The price of using money over time

It links today's money to tomorrow's.

cards.front: What usually happens when central banks raise rates?
cards.back:
Borrowing becomes more expensive and demand cools

It is a tool against inflation.

cards.front: What is a tariff?
cards.back:
A tax on imported goods

The customer usually pays part of it.

cards.front: What is GDP?
cards.back:
The value produced inside a country in a period

It is a flow, not a stock.

cards.front: Why do countries specialise?
cards.back:
They produce some goods at lower opportunity cost

Comparative advantage explains the gain.

cards.front: What is an opportunity cost?
cards.back:
The value of what you give up to choose something

Every choice has one.

cards.front: What does a price ceiling usually create?
cards.back:
Shortages

Demand rises above the capped supply.

cards.front: What is a stock and what is a flow?
cards.back:
A stock is a quantity; a flow is per unit of time

Debt is a stock, deficit a flow.

cards.front: Why is a diversified economy more resilient?
cards.back:
A shock to one sector hurts less

Concentration amplifies shocks.

items.title: Learning a language — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the learning a language guide.

cards.front: What should a beginner learn first in a new language?
cards.back:
The sounds that carry meaning

The ear guides the mouth.

cards.front: Why do frequency lists help beginners?
cards.back:
A few hundred words cover a large share of speech

Common words recur constantly.

cards.front: What makes vocabulary stick?
cards.back:
Meeting a word in several contexts

Context gives it hooks.

cards.front: What is a cognate?
cards.back:
A word that resembles one in another language

Resemblance can mislead.

cards.front: Why is speaking early useful?
cards.back:
Mistakes become correctable material

Feedback accelerates learning.

cards.front: What does spaced repetition optimise?
cards.back:
The timing of reviews

It exploits forgetting.

cards.front: What is a false friend?
cards.back:
A word that looks familiar but means something else

Spanish 'embarazada' is not embarrassed.

cards.front: Why does immersion accelerate learning?
cards.back:
The language is needed, not studied

Necessity drives attention.

cards.front: What helps listening comprehension most?
cards.back:
Hearing the same material at several speeds

Slow first, then natural speed.

cards.front: What is grammatical gender?
cards.back:
A noun class that affects agreement

It is only loosely tied to meaning.

items.title: How music works — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the how music works guide.

cards.front: What is rhythm in music?
cards.back:
The organisation of sound in time

Pulse, division and accent.

cards.front: What makes two notes consonant?
cards.back:
Their frequencies relate by a simple ratio

Octaves and fifths are simple.

cards.front: What is a scale?
cards.back:
An ordered set of notes used in a piece

Scales shape the mood.

cards.front: What does a chord do?
cards.back:
Sounds several notes together as a unit

Harmony is built from chords.

cards.front: What is a tempo?
cards.back:
The speed of the pulse

It is given in beats per minute.

cards.front: Why do pieces repeat material?
cards.back:
Repetition makes a form the listener can follow

Variation keeps attention.

cards.front: What is an octave?
cards.back:
The interval where one frequency is double the other

The notes sound alike.

cards.front: What does a key signature indicate?
cards.back:
Which notes belong to the piece by default

Accidentals mark exceptions.

cards.front: What is syncopation?
cards.back:
An accent placed off the expected beat

It drives dance music.

cards.front: Why does a melody get stuck in the head?
cards.back:
Short, repeated, slightly irregular patterns are memorable

Simplicity plus one surprise.

items.title: Food, energy and health — revision cards
items.description: Ten cards to revise the food, energy and health guide.

cards.front: What does a food label's energy value depend on?
cards.back:
The portion size it refers to

Always check the reference amount.

cards.front: Which nutrient provides the most energy per gram?
cards.back:
Fat

About nine kilocalories per gram.

cards.front: What does fibre do?
cards.back:
Feeds gut bacteria and slows sugar absorption

It is mostly not digested.

cards.front: Why is a single food rarely a health solution?
cards.back:
The whole diet and pattern matter more

Look at the week, not the meal.

cards.front: What is a calorie?
cards.back:
A unit of energy

On labels it means a kilocalorie.

cards.front: Why does protein matter after exercise?
cards.back:
It supplies the material to repair muscle

Spread across the day.

cards.front: What does hydration affect?
cards.back:
Blood volume and temperature regulation

Thirst arrives late.

cards.front: Why can portions be misjudged?
cards.back:
People estimate volume poorly without scales

Measuring once is informative.

cards.front: What is a balanced diet?
cards.back:
One supplying energy and nutrients in the right proportions

Variety is the practical rule.

cards.front: What does a 'light' product usually change?
cards.back:
One nutrient, often sugar or fat

Read the whole table.
